newsitem.title: GERMANY: Dutch premier says EMU needs Germany, France.
newsitem.headline: Dutch premier says EMU needs Germany, France.

text.p: European economic and monetary union (EMU), set to begin in 1999, can only be launched on time if Germany and France participate, Dutch Prime Minister Wim Kok told a German newspaper.

Responding to a reporter's question in an interview with the German weekly Die Zeit about what would happen if Germany failed to qualify for EMU, Kok said, "Then there would be no monetary union in 1999. That would also be true if France failed to qualify."

Despite doubts that Germany will be able to meet the strict limits on budget deficits outlined in the Maastricht treaty, Kok said the goal of all European Union members must be to "fulfil the criteria and to stick to the timetable."
The goal must be to launch EMU on January 1, 1999 with a group of countries that "fulfil the criteria without ifs or buts," he added.
Kok added there was still some flexibility to interpret the criteria in the Maastricht treaty. "It is enough if total debt is falling and approaching the entry mark," he said.
The Maastricht treaty states that total public debt should be limited to 60 percent of gross domestic product and budget deficits to three percent.
Commenting on the budget deficit limit, Kok said: "Three percent is three percent."
"A country whose budget deficit lies only one or two tenths above three percent will have to have very, very convincing arguments (to enter EMU)," he said.

"But on the other hand, the decision about who enters in the first round will not be made by computers. We will take a look at developments behind the numbers in April 1998 and not only consider the deficit and public debt, but also the total economic condition of a country and the solidity of its structural reforms."
